steps.explanationAfterStep: The α-silyl carbanion adds to the ketone like any organolithium.
Silicon takes a fifth ligand, closing a four-membered ring, like the oxaphosphetane in a Wittig.
Also accepted: a one-step syn-elimination, with the Si–O bond forming as the ring breaks. Whether the four-membered silicate is a true intermediate is debated.

The ring breaks into the alkene and Me₃SiO⁻. The strong Si–O bond pays for it. Because O and Si leave from the same side, the basic Peterson is a syn-elimination; in acid the β-hydroxysilane eliminates anti instead, so one diastereomer can give either alkene isomer. The app does not check that yet.

title: Peterson olefination
subtitle: (Trimethylsilyl)methyllithium turns cyclohexanone into methylenecyclohexane
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 27

alkoxide.caption: the β-silyl alkoxide (lithium salt)
hintTiers: Silicon forms very strong bonds to oxygen, and it can take a fifth bond. Which atom is three bonds from the alkoxide oxygen?
One arrow: the alkoxide lone pair forms a new bond to silicon, closing a four-membered ring.
Alkoxide lone pair → new bond to silicon.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Oxygen bonds to silicon, not to a carbon. The Si–O bond is one of the strongest single bonds.
That just undoes the addition. Bond the oxygen to silicon.

silicate.caption: a four-membered ring with a five-coordinate silicate
hintTiers: Break the two ring bonds that are not Si–O: the C–Si bond becomes the C=C π bond.
Two arrows: the C–Si bond → the C=C π bond; the C–O bond → a lone pair on oxygen.
Si–CH₂ bond → C=C π bond; ring C–O bond → a lone pair on oxygen.
silicate.learnerPrompt: The ring breaks into an alkene and a silanolate.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That reopens the ring to the alkoxide. Keep the Si–O bond: break C–Si and C–O.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the C=C bond forms. That carbon now has five bonds: break the C–O bond onto oxygen.

reactants.caption: (trimethylsilyl)methyllithium + cyclohexanone
hintTiers: The C–Li bond is very polar: the carbon is a nucleophile, stabilised a little by the silicon next to it. Where is the electrophile?
The C–Li bonding pair forms the new C–C bond to the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π pair moves onto oxygen. Two arrows.
C–Li bond → new bond from that carbon to the carbonyl carbon; C=O π bond → a lone pair on oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: The organolithium adds to the ketone.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The carbonyl oxygen is the electron-rich end. The carbon nucleophile bonds to the carbonyl carbon.
The C=O π pair goes to oxygen, not to carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the new C–C bond. Now move the C=O π pair onto oxygen.

mechanismSummary: The α-silyl organolithium adds to the ketone. The β-silyl alkoxide attacks silicon, giving a four-membered ring, which breaks into the alkene and trimethylsilanolate: the silicon version of the Wittig, driven by the strong Si–O bond. With lithium the alkoxide eliminates slowly, so the β-hydroxysilane is often isolated after work-up and then treated with KH (syn-elimination) or acid (anti-elimination).
